entry.title: Saffron Pappardelle with Wild Porcini and Walnut Crema
entry.content:
Introduction

Benvenuti! Right now, the air in Tuscany is changing—the scent of damp earth and woodsmoke signals the arrival of the festival season. Today, I am bringing the spirit of the Sagra del Fungo Porcino directly to your table. We are making a dish that marries the golden vibrance of saffron with the deep, meaty soul of the forest. It is a celebration of the harvest, using only what the land provides: flour, water, ancient spice, and the king of the woods. This is slow food for a fast world, rooted in the hills I call home.

Ingredients

  • 200g '00' flour
  • 100g semolina flour, plus extra for dusting
  • 1/2 teaspoon saffron threads, soaked in 100ml warm water
  • 1 tablespoon extra virgin olive oil (plus more for finishing)
  • 300g fresh porcini mushrooms (or king oyster mushrooms), sliced thick
  • 2 garlic cloves, smashed
  • 1/2 cup walnuts, toasted and very finely crushed
  • 1 sprig of fresh thyme
  • 1/4 cup dry white wine
  • Sea salt and cracked black pepper to taste

Instructions

  • On a clean wooden surface, mix the '00' and semolina flours into a mound. Create a deep well in the center.
  • Pour the saffron water (and threads) and a tablespoon of olive oil into the well. Using a fork, gradually incorporate the flour from the edges until a shaggy dough forms.
  • Knead the dough by hand for 10 minutes until it is smooth, elastic, and glowing gold. Wrap in a damp cloth and rest for 30 minutes.
  • Roll the dough out thinly and cut into wide ribbons—about 2cm across—to create your pappardelle. Dust with semolina to prevent sticking.
  • In a wide pan, heat a generous glug of olive oil over medium-high heat. Add the mushrooms in a single layer. Let them brown undisturbed for 3 minutes to develop a deep crust.
  • Add the smashed garlic and thyme sprigs. Toss gently, then deglaze the pan with the white wine, scraping up the flavorful bits from the bottom.
  • Stir in the crushed walnuts and a ladle of starchy pasta water to create a creamy, emulsified sauce. Remove the garlic cloves.
  • Boil the pappardelle in salted water for only 2-3 minutes. Transfer them directly into the mushroom pan using tongs.
  • Toss everything together over low heat, adding a splash more pasta water if needed. Finish with a heavy drizzle of your best new-press olive oil and cracked pepper.

There is no secret to this dish other than the quality of your oil and the patience in your hands. Serve it while the steam still carries the scent of the woods, and perhaps share it with someone who appreciates the beauty of a meal grown from the earth. A tavola a mangiare!

Isabella

Additional Information
NutritionfactsCalories: 480kcal, Fat: 22g, Carbohydrates: 58g, Protein: 14g, Fiber: 5g
Preparation Time1 hour
Allergy InformationGluten (Wheat), Tree Nuts (Walnuts)
Yield2 servings

entry.title: Red Wine Miso Braised Daikon with Truffled Edamame Silk
entry.content:
Introduction

As the frost settles on the temple gardens, the winter daikon reaches its peak sweetness. This dish is a quiet dialogue between the slow, patient braising techniques of the West and the deep umami of our house-aged red miso. It is a meditation on time, gravity, and the earth's quiet transition into winter.

Ingredients

  • 1 large winter daikon (approx 1kg), peeled and cut into 4cm rounds
  • 500ml Kombu dashi (cold-extracted overnight)
  • 200ml Vegan dry red wine (such as a Japanese Muscat Bailey A or Pinot Noir)
  • 3 tbsp Aged red miso (Aka Miso)
  • 2 tbsp Tamari (aged)
  • 1 piece Dried kombu (5cm square)
  • 200g Fresh edamame, shelled
  • 1 tsp Black truffle oil or fresh truffle shavings
  • 10cm Burdock root (gobo), shaved into thin ribbons
  • Small handful of micro-shiso or seasonal purple flowers
  • 1 tsp Organic coconut sugar

Instructions

  • Begin by beveling the edges of the daikon rounds (mentori) with a sharp knife to prevent them from breaking during the long simmer.
  • Parboil the daikon in rice-wash water (togijiru) for 15 minutes to remove any bitterness, then rinse gently in cold water.
  • In a heavy bottomed ceramic pot, combine the kombu dashi, red wine, tamari, and the piece of kombu. Place the daikon rounds in a single layer.
  • Bring to a very faint simmer. Cover with an otoshibuta (drop lid) and cook on the lowest heat possible for 90 minutes. The daikon should become translucent and dark with the wine.
  • In the final 15 minutes, whisk the red miso and coconut sugar with a little of the braising liquid until smooth, then stir it back into the pot. Let it glaze the radish slowly.
  • While the daikon rests, steam the edamame for 5 minutes. Blend with a splash of dashi and truffle oil until it reaches a silken, airy consistency.
  • Flash-fry the shaved burdock ribbons in a neutral oil until golden and crisp, mimicking the flavor of binchotan smoke.
  • To plate, place a generous sweep of the green edamame silk on an asymmetric ceramic plate. Position one daikon round slightly off-center. Top with a nest of crispy burdock and a single shiso bud.

Eat with presence. Feel the warmth of the binchotan-kissed burdock and the depth of the fermented miso. In this bowl, the seasons meet and find stillness. May it nourish your spirit as much as your body.

Hiroshi

Additional Information
NutritionfactsCalories: 245kcal, Protein: 9g, Carbohydrates: 22g, Fiber: 7g, Fat: 6g, Sodium: 840mg.
Preparation Time2 hours 15 minutes
Allergy InformationSoy (Miso, Tamari, Edamame)
Yield4 servings

entry.title: Sun-Drenched Masa and Smoky Heirloom Bean Bake
entry.content:
Introduction

There is a specific kind of magic that happens when the late afternoon sun hits a table in the Bay Area, and this baked meze is my tribute to those golden hours. It’s a dish that bridges the gap between a rugged coastal fire and a refined wine-country kitchen. By combining the earthy, grounding texture of heirloom beans with the bright, citrusy lift of Ojai lemons and the smoky depth of Central Valley chiles, we create something that feels both deeply rooted and effortlessly light. This isn't just a snack; it's a celebration of the soil and the sea, designed to be shared with friends while the salt air drifts through the window.

Ingredients

  • 2 cups cooked heirloom pinto beans, drained
  • 1 cup organic masa harina
  • 1/2 cup warm filtered water
  • 1/4 cup premium Sonoma olive oil
  • 1 cup heirloom cherry tomatoes, halved
  • 2 tablespoons chipotle in adobo, finely minced
  • 1 teaspoon flaky sea salt
  • Zest and juice of 1 Ojai lemon
  • 1/4 cup toasted pepitas (pumpkin seeds)
  • 1/2 cup vegan almond-based feta, crumbled
  • 1/4 cup fresh cilantro leaves, torn
  • 1/4 cup fresh mint leaves, torn
  • 1 teaspoon cracked black pepper

Instructions

  • Preheat your oven to 400°F (200°C). If you have access to a wood-fired oven, use almond wood for a sweet, nutty smoke.
  • In a small mixing bowl, combine the masa harina with a pinch of salt and the warm water. Knead gently until a smooth dough forms. Roll the dough into small, marble-sized balls and flatten them slightly with your thumb to create small dimples.
  • In a shallow ceramic baking dish, toss the pinto beans with the Sonoma olive oil, minced chipotle in adobo, and sea salt until evenly coated.
  • Nestle the prepared masa disks and the halved cherry tomatoes into the bean mixture, ensuring some of the beans are still peeking through.
  • Place the dish in the oven and bake for 22 to 25 minutes. You are looking for the tomatoes to burst and caramelize, and the masa disks to become golden and crisp around the edges.
  • Remove from the oven and immediately zest the Ojai lemon over the top while it’s still sizzling.
  • Sprinkle with the crumbled vegan feta, toasted pepitas, and cracked black pepper.
  • Finish the dish by showering it with fresh cilantro and mint, and a final generous drizzle of olive oil.
  • Serve warm directly from the dish with charred corn tortillas or simply a spoon.

I hope this dish brings a little bit of that California sunshine to your table today. Whether you are dipping a warm tortilla into the smoky beans or savoring a crisp masa dumpling, remember that the best food is always a reflection of the landscape and the people we share it with. Keep it simple, keep it seasonal, and always use the best olive oil you can find. Happy cooking!

Emily

Additional Information
Nutritionfacts320 calories, 12g protein, 42g carbohydrates, 14g fat, 9g fiber per serving.
Preparation Time45 minutes
Allergy InformationContains seeds (pepitas) and nuts (almond-based feta). Gluten-free.
Yield4 servings

entry.title: 72-Hour Fermented Masa and Heirloom Tomato Galette
entry.content:
Introduction

There is a quiet magic that happens when you let dough breathe and mature. Taking inspiration from the aged pastry trend hitting the artisanal bakeries of the Mission District, I have combined my love for sourdough with the deep, earthy soul of nixtamalized masa. This crust ferments for three days, developing a complex tang that perfectly anchors the sweetness of sun-drenched heirloom tomatoes and smoky peaches. It is a slice of the California coast—rugged, golden, and deeply flavored.

Ingredients

  • 1 cup active sourdough starter
  • 1 1/2 cups organic all-purpose flour
  • 1/2 cup heirloom blue or yellow masa harina
  • 3/4 cup cold-pressed solid coconut oil or vegan cultured butter
  • 1 teaspoon sea salt
  • 2 tablespoons ice-cold verjus or apple cider vinegar
  • 3 large heirloom tomatoes, sliced thick
  • 1 ripe Ojai peach, thinly sliced
  • 1 Fresno chile, seeded and minced
  • 2 tablespoons Sonoma olive oil
  • 1 bunch fresh purple basil and cilantro
  • Flaky sea salt and cracked black pepper
  • 1 teaspoon smoky adobo sauce for brushing

Instructions

  • In a large bowl, whisk together the flour, masa harina, and sea salt. Cut in the cold fat until it resembles coarse crumbs.
  • Fold in the sourdough starter and ice-cold verjus. Knead very gently until a shaggy dough forms.
  • Wrap the dough tightly and refrigerate for 48 to 72 hours. This aging process allows the sourdough and masa to develop a deep, fermented flavor profile.
  • When ready to bake, preheat your oven to 425°F (220°C). If you have a baking stone or steel, use it to mimic a wood-fired floor.
  • Roll the aged dough out on parchment paper into a rough 12-inch circle. The edges should be rustic and uneven.
  • Layer the tomato and peach slices in the center, leaving a 2-inch border. Sprinkle with the minced Fresno chile and a drizzle of olive oil.
  • Fold the edges of the dough over the fruit, overlapping where necessary. Brush the crust with a mixture of olive oil and a drop of adobo sauce for a smoky glow.
  • Bake for 30-35 minutes until the crust is deeply golden and the tomatoes have slumped and concentrated their sugars.
  • Top with fresh herbs and flaky salt immediately before serving.

Take this galette outside, find a patch of shade under an oak tree, and share it with friends. The way the aged masa crust shatters against the juicy tomatoes is why I love cooking in the Bay—it is simple, honest, and purely of the earth.

Emily

Additional Information
NutritionfactsCalories: 310kcal, Carbohydrates: 38g, Protein: 5g, Fat: 16g, Fiber: 4g
Preparation Time72 hours plus 45 minutes
Allergy InformationGluten, Corn
Yield6 slices

entry.title: Charred Coconut Cassava Cakes with Berbere Tamarind Glaze
entry.content:
Introduction

Habari! Today, I’m bringing the warmth of the Mombasa sun to your kitchen. This snack celebrates the humble cassava, transformed by the sizzle of a hot tava and the deep, complex heat of Ethiopian berbere. It is a bite of the coast and the highlands all in one, perfectly capturing the Indian Ocean breeze and the red soil of our home.

Ingredients

  • 2 cups grated fresh cassava (muhogo), moisture squeezed out
  • 1/2 cup thick coconut milk, pressed fresh
  • 1 tablespoon berbere spice blend
  • 1 teaspoon toasted cumin seeds
  • 2 green pilipili chiles, finely minced
  • 2 tablespoons tamarind paste
  • 1 tablespoon coconut sugar or maple syrup
  • 1/2 cup roasted groundnuts, crushed for topping
  • Fresh coriander and lime wedges for garnish
  • Sea salt to taste
  • Coconut oil for searing

Instructions

  • In a large bowl, combine the grated cassava with the coconut milk, minced chiles, cumin seeds, and a pinch of salt. Mix until a thick, moldable dough forms.
  • Shape the mixture into small, flat round cakes, approximately 2 inches in diameter.
  • In a small bowl, whisk together the tamarind paste, berbere spice, and coconut sugar to create a thick glaze.
  • Heat a tava or heavy cast-iron skillet over medium-high heat and lightly coat with coconut oil.
  • Place the cassava cakes on the skillet and sear for 4 to 5 minutes per side until a golden-brown, crispy crust develops.
  • Brush the top of each cake generously with the berbere tamarind glaze and cook for one additional minute to allow it to caramelize.
  • Remove from the heat and immediately sprinkle with crushed groundnuts and fresh coriander.

Serve these while the warmth of the pan still lingers. A squeeze of lime and a handful of fresh kachumbari on the side is all you need to transport yourself to the shores of Mombasa. Karibuni!

Nia

Additional Information
NutritionfactsPer serving: 185 kcal, 9g fat, 24g carbohydrates, 3g protein, 4g fiber.
Preparation Time30 minutes
Allergy InformationGroundnuts (Peanuts)
Yield12 cakes

entry.title: Grilled Nopales and Al Dente Heirloom Bean Tostaditas
entry.content:
Introduction

Hey there! This morning at the market, the nopales were perfectly firm and the heirloom beans looked like little gems. I wanted to create something that captures that al dente bite—something with texture, soul, and a bit of crunch. These tostaditas are a coastal California love letter: smoky from the almond wood grill, bright with Ojai citrus, and deeply satisfying. It is exactly the kind of unfussy, sun-drenched snack I love to share after a morning in the surf.

Ingredients

  • 1 cup dried heirloom pinto or Flor de Mayo beans, soaked overnight
  • 2 large fresh nopal paddles, thorns removed and edges trimmed
  • 1 cup sun-ripened cherry tomatoes, halved
  • 2 ears of Central Valley sweet corn, husks removed
  • 1/4 cup Sonoma extra virgin olive oil
  • 2 tablespoons verjus or fresh lemon juice
  • 1 tablespoon chipotle in adobo, finely minced
  • 1 teaspoon preserved lemon peel, minced
  • 12 small corn tortillas (hand-pressed masa if possible)
  • A handful of fresh cilantro and opal basil leaves
  • Flaky sea salt and smoked paprika to taste

Instructions

  • Simmer the soaked heirloom beans in salted water with a clove of garlic until they are tender but still offer a distinct bite, about 45 to 60 minutes. Drain and set aside to cool.
  • Prepare your grill over almond wood or medium-high heat. Brush the corn and nopal paddles with a little olive oil.
  • Grill the corn until charred in spots and the nopales until they turn olive green and have beautiful grill marks (about 4 minutes per side).
  • Dice the grilled nopales into 1/2-inch cubes and shear the sweet corn kernels off the cob.
  • In a large bowl, whisk together the Sonoma olive oil, verjus, minced chipotle, and preserved lemon.
  • Fold in the al dente beans, grilled nopales, corn, and cherry tomatoes. Let the flavors marry for 10 minutes.
  • Lightly brush the corn tortillas with oil and grill or toast them until crisp and golden.
  • Spoon the vibrant bean and cactus mixture onto each crisp tortilla.
  • Finish with a scatter of fresh herbs, a dusting of smoked paprika, and a final sprinkle of flaky sea salt.

I hope this brings a bit of that Golden State sunshine to your kitchen. Grab a glass of chilled verjus or a local pét-nat, find a sunlit spot on the porch, and enjoy every vibrant crunch. There is nothing like the snap of fresh produce to make the day feel special. Happy cooking!

Emily

Additional Information
NutritionfactsPer serving (3 tostaditas): 310 calories, 12g fat, 44g carbs, 10g protein, 9g fiber.
Preparation Time1 hour 15 minutes
Allergy InformationNone (Naturally gluten-free and vegan; ensure corn tortillas are 100% corn)
Yield12 tostaditas (serves 4 as tapas)

entry.title: Crispy Smashed Potatoes with Porcini and Rosemary Dust
entry.content:
Introduction

Benvenuti! Today, I am bringing the earthy soul of my Tuscan woods to a modern small-plate tradition. These potatoes are boiled until tender, smashed, and roasted until they shatter between your teeth. The secret is the 'dust'—a concentrated powder of dried porcini mushrooms and wild rosemary that coats every golden crevice with pure umami. It is a humble garden staple transformed into a sophisticated, dusted tapas bite.

Ingredients

  • 800g small baby potatoes (yellow or red)
  • 30g dried porcini mushrooms
  • 1 tablespoon fresh rosemary needles, finely chopped
  • 1 teaspoon coarse sea salt
  • 1 tablespoon nutritional yeast
  • 4 tablespoons extra virgin olive oil
  • Freshly cracked black pepper

Instructions

  • Place the potatoes in a large pot of salted water and bring to a boil. Cook for 15-20 minutes until fork-tender.
  • While the potatoes boil, place the dried porcini mushrooms in a high-speed blender or spice grinder. Pulse until they become a fine powder.
  • In a small bowl, mix the porcini powder with the salt, nutritional yeast, and finely chopped rosemary. This is your 'dust'.
  • Preheat your oven to 220C (425F).
  • Drain the potatoes and let them steam dry for 2 minutes to ensure maximum crispiness. Place them on a lined baking sheet.
  • Use a flat-bottomed glass to gently press down on each potato until it is about 1cm thick but still holds together.
  • Drizzle generously with extra virgin olive oil and sprinkle with half of the porcini-rosemary dust.
  • Roast for 25-30 minutes, flipping halfway through, until the edges are deep golden brown.
  • Remove from the oven and immediately toss with the remaining dust while the oil is still sizzling so it sticks to the skins.

Serve these while they are still hot enough to warm your fingertips. A drizzle of your best new-press olive oil at the end is not a suggestion—it is a requirement! Simple, honest, and perfect for sharing. Buon appetito!

Isabella

Additional Information
NutritionfactsPer serving: 210 kcal, 4g Protein, 28g Carbs, 9g Fat, 4g Fiber.
Preparation Time45 minutes
Allergy InformationNone
Yield4 servings

entry.title: Tuscan Polenta Fries with Sun-Dried Tomato Tapenade
entry.content:
Introduction

Benvenuti! This dish is a love letter to the cucina povera, where we transform the humblest cornmeal into a celebration worthy of a piazza feast. In the spirit of today's reduced food festival, we honor the philosophy of using what we have—stale-stored polenta and the intense, sun-drenched preserves of last season—to create something crunchy, salty, and soulful.

Ingredients

  • 250g coarse cornmeal (polenta)
  • 1 liter water
  • 1 tsp sea salt
  • 3 sprigs fresh rosemary, needles removed
  • 100g sun-dried tomatoes in oil, drained (reserve the oil)
  • 1 tbsp capers, rinsed
  • 1 small clove garlic, peeled
  • Zest of one organic lemon
  • Extra virgin olive oil for frying

Instructions

  • Bring the water to a rolling boil in a heavy-bottomed pot and add the sea salt.
  • Slowly whisk in the cornmeal in a steady stream to avoid lumps, then reduce the heat to low.
  • Stir the polenta regularly with a wooden spoon for about 35 to 40 minutes until it is thick and pulls away cleanly from the sides of the pot.
  • Pour the hot polenta onto a parchment-lined tray, smoothing it to a thickness of 2cm. Allow it to cool and set completely for at least one hour.
  • While the polenta sets, create the tapenade by pounding the sun-dried tomatoes, capers, garlic, and lemon zest in a mortar and pestle until a rustic paste forms. Stir in a little of the reserved tomato oil for silkiness.
  • Once the polenta is firm, cut it into thick batons or wedges.
  • Heat a generous layer of olive oil in a wide skillet. Toss in the rosemary needles to infuse the oil until they are fragrant.
  • Fry the polenta batons in batches until each side is deeply golden and remarkably crispy. Drain them on a clean kitchen cloth.
  • Serve the warm fries immediately with the tapenade on the side for dipping.

Serve these golden treasures while the sun sets over the hills, perhaps with a glass of chilled Vermentino. It is the taste of the Tuscan spring, shared with love and a spirit that knows nothing is ever truly wasted. Buon appetito!

Isabella

Additional Information
NutritionfactsPer serving: 240 kcal, 12g Fat, 30g Carbs, 4g Protein, 5g Fiber
Preparation Time1 hour 45 minutes
Allergy InformationNone
Yield4 servings

entry.title: Yuzu-Kama Silken Tofu with Binchotan-Charred Miso
entry.content:
Introduction

Welcome. Today, we listen to the voice of the yuzu at its absolute shun. This dish is a quiet meditation on the transition from winter’s depth to the first breath of spring. By hollowing the fruit and lightly kissing it with binchotan flame, we release an aroma that clears the mind before the first bite of our morning-made silken tofu.

Ingredients

  • 2 large firm-skinned organic yuzu or sudachi
  • 200g fresh silken tofu crafted this morning
  • 100ml ichiban kombu dashi cold-extracted for 12 hours
  • 1 tablespoon artisanal white miso fermented in-house
  • 1 teaspoon aged tamari
  • 1 teaspoon organic mirin
  • 1 small segment of dekopon citrus for natural sweetness
  • 2 micro-shiso leaves or hanaho shiso flowers
  • A pinch of fresh yuzu zest

Instructions

  • Carefully slice the top third of the yuzu to create a lid and hollow out the fruit using a small spoon, reserving two teaspoons of the juice.
  • Hold the empty yuzu shells with bamboo tongs over glowing binchotan charcoal for 20 seconds until the skin expresses its oils and smells toasted.
  • In a small copper pot, whisk the white miso, tamari, and mirin over low heat until the mixture thickens into a glossy glaze.
  • Warm the silken tofu gently in the kombu dashi at exactly 70 degrees Celsius, ensuring the texture remains like custard.
  • Place a portion of the warm tofu inside each charred yuzu shell and add one small segment of dekopon.
  • Spoon the miso glaze over the tofu and place the yuzu lid slightly ajar.
  • Steam the entire vessel for exactly three minutes to infuse the tofu with the citrus fragrance.
  • Finish with a drop of fresh yuzu juice, a dusting of zest, and a single shiso flower for balance.

As you finish this small offering, notice how the bitterness of the charred rind lingers softly against the sweetness of the miso. It is a reminder that beauty often resides in the fleeting and the imperfect. May this citrus warmth stay with you throughout your day.

Hiroshi

Additional Information
NutritionfactsCalories: 85, Protein: 5g, Fat: 3g, Carbohydrates: 9g, Fiber: 2g
Preparation Time25 minutes
Allergy InformationSoy
Yield2 servings

entry.title: Smoky Adobo Mushroom Sliders with Charred Tomato Jam
entry.content:
Introduction

Hey there! Today we’re bringing the soul of a foggy coastal pub right into the sunshine. Think of these as the ultimate Northern California handhelds—meaty grilled mushrooms drenched in a sun-drenched adobo, tucked into toasted masa buns. It’s smoky, bright, and perfect for sharing with a crisp glass of local pét-nat or a chilled verjus sparkler. This is unfussy coastal comfort at its finest.

Ingredients

  • 1 lb King Trumpet and Oyster mushrooms, torn into bite-sized strips
  • 2 tbsp Sonoma extra virgin olive oil
  • 1/4 cup chipotle in adobo sauce, pureed
  • 1 tsp smoked paprika
  • 2 cloves garlic, minced
  • 6 small slider-sized masa buns or sourdough rolls
  • 2 large heirloom tomatoes, sliced 1/2-inch thick
  • 1 tbsp verjus or fresh lemon juice
  • 1/2 cup vegan avocado-oil aioli
  • 1 tbsp non-pareil capers, roughly chopped
  • 1/4 cup fresh cilantro and Italian parsley, finely minced
  • 1 ripe Hass avocado, thinly sliced
  • Handful of pickled Fresno chiles
  • Flaky sea salt and cracked black pepper to taste

Instructions

  • Preheat a heavy cast-iron skillet or an outdoor grill over medium-high heat. If you can, use almond wood for a sweet, nutty smoke profile.
  • In a large bowl, whisk together the olive oil, adobo sauce, smoked paprika, and minced garlic.
  • Toss the torn mushrooms in the adobo mixture until every crevice is coated.
  • Sear the mushrooms in the hot skillet or on a grill basket until the edges are crispy and charred, about 8 to 10 minutes, stirring occasionally.
  • While the mushrooms cook, place the heirloom tomato slices directly on the grill or a separate hot pan for 60 seconds per side until they show char marks. Transfer to a small bowl and mash gently with the verjus and a pinch of salt to create a chunky, rustic jam.
  • In a small ramekin, fold the chopped capers and fresh herbs into the vegan aioli.
  • Split the buns and toast them lightly until golden.
  • Build the sliders by spreading a thick layer of the herb-caper aioli on the bottom bun. Pile on the smoky mushrooms, followed by a spoonful of the charred tomato jam.
  • Top with a slice of avocado and a few pickled Fresno chiles for a hit of acid and heat.
  • Serve immediately while the mushrooms are still sizzling.

There you have it—a little piece of the Pacific coast on a plate. This dish is all about the layers: the deep wood-fired char, the sweetness of the heirloom tomatoes, and that creamy, briny herb finish. Pull up a chair, grab a cold drink, and enjoy the peak of the season. Stay sun-drenched, friends!

Emily

Additional Information
NutritionfactsCalories: 340, Total Fat: 18g, Saturated Fat: 2.5g, Sodium: 520mg, Total Carbohydrates: 38g, Dietary Fiber: 7g, Sugars: 6g, Protein: 9g
Preparation Time45 minutes
Allergy InformationContains Gluten (if using sourdough), Nightshades (tomatoes/chiles), Soy (check aioli ingredients).
Yield6 sliders

entry.title: Shojin Harvest Pizza with Binchotan Maitake and Shiro Miso Cream
entry.content:
Introduction

In the quiet corners of Kyoto, we learn that even a dish as global as pizza can become a vessel for shojin ryori. Today, I offer you a meditation on fire and fermentation. This artisan pizza honors the essence of shun by using earth-grown ingredients treated with the reverence of a temple meal. We use a slow-fermented sourdough to mirror the patience of the seasons, topped with treasures from the forest floor charred over binchotan coals. It is a warm, rustic embrace that celebrates the harmony between tradition and the present moment.

Ingredients

  • 250g Sourdough pizza dough, 72-hour cold fermented
  • 100g Maitake mushrooms, hand-torn to preserve texture
  • 50g Takenoko (young bamboo shoots), sliced paper-thin using katsuramuki technique
  • 3 tbsp Shiro miso (white miso), house-fermented
  • 100ml Silken tofu, pressed and blended into a smooth cream
  • 1 sheet Fresh Yuba (bean curd skin), torn into delicate ribbons
  • 1 tsp Sansho pepper berries, lightly bruised
  • 1 tbsp Kombu-infused extra virgin olive oil
  • A handful of fresh Mizuna or Shiso leaves
  • A pinch of flaked sea salt

Instructions

  • Begin by preheating a pizza stone in your oven at its highest setting for at least one hour, or prepare your binchotan charcoal grill for high-heat indirect cooking.
  • Lightly sear the maitake mushrooms and bamboo shoots over the binchotan coals until the edges are curled and kissed with smoke.
  • In a small cedar bowl, whisk the shiro miso into the silken tofu cream until it reaches the consistency of a thick, pale velvet.
  • On a floured surface, gently stretch the sourdough dough by hand, being careful not to bruise the air pockets earned through long fermentation.
  • Spread the miso-tofu cream over the base in a thin, intentional layer, leaving a wide margin for the crust to rise.
  • Arrange the smoked mushrooms, bamboo shoots, and yuba ribbons across the cream in an asymmetrical, natural pattern.
  • Slide the pizza onto the hot stone and bake until the crust is blistered with leopard spots and the yuba has turned slightly crisp.
  • Remove from the heat and immediately drizzle with the kombu-infused oil and a dusting of sansho pepper.
  • Garnish with fresh greens just before serving to maintain their vibrant life force.

As you finish this meal, take a moment to appreciate the charcoal’s breath and the grain’s transformation. This pizza is not merely food, but a dialogue between the element of fire and the gift of the earth. I hope it brings a sense of wabi-sabi to your table—perfect in its imperfections. Until the seasons shift again, keep your heart open and your dashi clear.

Hiroshi

Additional Information
Nutritionfacts420 kcal, 12g Protein, 58g Carbohydrates, 14g Fat, 6g Fiber, Probiotic-rich.
Preparation Time25 minutes (excluding dough fermentation)
Allergy InformationSoy, Wheat (Gluten)
Yield1 individual 12-inch pizza

entry.title: Swahili Coastal Croquettes with Berbere-Tamarind Glaze
entry.content:
Introduction

Karibu! In my Mombasa kitchen, the air always smells of salt and roasting spices. Today, I am bringing the red soil of the highlands and the blue of the Indian Ocean together in a single bite. These croquettes transform the humble, earthy njahi bean and creamy cassava into a sophisticated finger food, spiked with the fiery warmth of berbere and cooled by the morning's fresh coconut milk. They are small, punchy, and perfect for sharing as the sun begins to dip below the horizon.

Ingredients

  • 2 cups boiled and mashed cassava root
  • 1 cup cooked njahi (black beans), lightly crushed
  • 2 green pilipili chiles, finely minced
  • 1 teaspoon toasted cumin seeds
  • 1 teaspoon ground cardamom
  • 1/2 cup sukuma wiki (collard greens), very finely shredded
  • 1/2 cup roasted groundnuts, crushed into a coarse meal
  • 2 tablespoons tamarind paste
  • 1 teaspoon berbere spice blend
  • 1 tablespoon coconut sugar
  • 1/2 cup thick fresh coconut milk
  • Juice of 1 lime
  • A pinch of sea salt

Instructions

  • In a large clay bowl, combine the mashed cassava, crushed njahi beans, pilipili chiles, cumin, cardamom, and shredded sukuma wiki until well incorporated.
  • Season the mixture with a pinch of sea salt and mix thoroughly.
  • Roll the mixture into small, bite-sized cylinders or rounds, about the size of a walnut.
  • Dredge each croquette in the crushed roasted groundnuts, pressing firmly so the nuts adhere to create a textured crust.
  • Heat a shallow layer of oil in a tava or heavy pan over medium heat. Fry the croquettes until they are golden brown and crispy on all sides.
  • In a small bowl, whisk together the tamarind paste, berbere spice, and coconut sugar to create a thick glaze.
  • Lightly brush the warm croquettes with the berbere-tamarind glaze while they are still hot.
  • For the dipping sauce, whisk the fresh coconut milk with lime juice and a tiny pinch of salt.
  • Arrange the croquettes on a platter and serve immediately with the coconut-lime dip on the side.

These bites are more than just food; they are the story of our trade winds and our resilient earth. I hope they bring a bit of the Swahili coast’s warmth to your table today. Serve them hot, share them widely, and let the spices linger. Until next time, stay seasoned.

Nia

Additional Information
NutritionfactsCalories: 210, Protein: 7g, Fiber: 6g, Fat: 9g (from groundnuts and coconut).
Preparation Time45 minutes
Allergy InformationGroundnuts (Peanuts)
Yield24 croquettes

entry.title: Smoky Adobo and Citrus Chewy Mushroom Steaks
entry.content:
Introduction

Hey there, friend! Today we are leaning into that incredible chewy texture that makes plant-based cooking so satisfying. I found some gorgeous King Oyster mushrooms at the market this morning, and they are the perfect canvas for a deep, smoky marinade inspired by the Central Valley. By scoring the mushrooms and searing them slow under a heavy press, we create a concentrated, bouncy bite that feels just like a sun-drenched afternoon in a coastal surf-town kitchen. Let's get grilling!

Ingredients

  • 1 lb King Oyster mushrooms, sliced into 1/2-inch thick planks
  • 3 tbsp chipotle peppers in adobo sauce, finely minced
  • 1/4 cup fresh Ojai orange juice
  • 2 tbsp Sonoma extra-virgin olive oil
  • 1 tbsp agave nectar or maple syrup
  • 2 cloves garlic, microplaned
  • 1 tsp dried Mexican oregano, crushed between palms
  • 1/2 tsp smoked paprika
  • Flaky sea salt and cracked black pepper
  • Fresh cilantro and lime wedges for serving
  • Warm heirloom masa tortillas

Instructions

  • Use a sharp knife to score a crosshatch pattern into both sides of the mushroom planks, being careful not to cut all the way through. This allows the chewy marinade to penetrate deep into the fibers.
  • In a wide shallow bowl, whisk together the minced chipotle, orange juice, olive oil, agave, garlic, oregano, and smoked paprika until a thick glaze forms.
  • Toss the mushroom planks in the marinade, ensuring every crevice is coated. Let them marinate at room temperature for at least 30 minutes.
  • Heat a heavy cast-iron skillet or a grill over medium-high heat (ideally over almond wood for that authentic NorCal aroma).
  • Place the mushrooms in the hot pan. Use a second heavy skillet or a grill press to weigh them down. This compression is key to achieving that signature chewy, condensed texture.
  • Sear for 5 minutes per side, or until the edges are charred and the marinade has caramelized into a sticky lacquer.
  • During the last minute of cooking, brush any remaining marinade over the top and let it bubble.
  • Transfer to a wooden board, sprinkle with flaky sea salt, and serve immediately with warm tortillas and a bright squeeze of lime.

I love serving these right off the cast iron while they are still sticky and hot. Pair them with a crisp glass of Sonoma white wine or a chilled verjus sparkler. It is unfussy, coastal, and exactly what a summer lunch should be. Enjoy the chew!

Emily

Additional Information

Preparation Time45 minutes
Allergy InformationNone
Yield4 servings

entry.title: Crema Dorata di Zucca e Cannellini
entry.content:
Introduction

Benvenuti to my kitchen. Today, my garden offers the last of the winter squash and the velvet creaminess of our local cannellini beans. This 'mashed sauce' is a tribute to the simplicity of my Tuscan hills—rich, textured, and kissed by the fire. It is a dish that honors the cucina povera tradition where we find luxury in the humble earth.

Ingredients

  • 600g butternut squash, peeled and cut into small cubes
  • 250g cooked cannellini beans, rinsed and drained
  • 4 cloves of garlic, kept in their skins
  • 120ml extra virgin olive oil, plus more for roasting
  • 10-12 fresh sage leaves
  • 60g toasted hazelnuts, roughly crushed
  • Zest of one organic lemon
  • Fine sea salt and freshly cracked black pepper to taste

Instructions

  • Preheat your oven to 200°C (400°F). Toss the squash cubes and the whole garlic cloves with a generous glug of olive oil and a pinch of salt on a baking sheet.
  • Roast for 25-30 minutes until the squash is tender and the edges are starting to caramelize into a deep gold.
  • Squeeze the softened roasted garlic out of its skins into a large stone mortar or a heavy ceramic bowl.
  • Add the roasted squash and the cannellini beans to the garlic. Use a potato masher or a heavy fork to crush the ingredients together until you have a thick, rustic, and chunky mash.
  • Gradually stir in the 120ml of extra virgin olive oil and the lemon zest, mixing until the sauce looks glossy and holds its shape.
  • In a small skillet, heat a tablespoon of oil over medium heat and flash-fry the sage leaves for about 30 seconds until crisp but still green.
  • Season the mash with salt and pepper, fold in half of the crushed hazelnuts, and top with the remaining hazelnuts and the crispy sage before serving.

Serve this over thick, handmade pappardelle or simply spread it on toasted pane di campagna. A drizzle of your best new-press olive oil is the only jewelry it needs. It is simple, honest, and soul-warming. Buon appetito!

Isabella

Additional Information
NutritionfactsCalories: 310, Fat: 19g, Carbohydrates: 32g, Protein: 7g, Fiber: 9g
Preparation Time45 minutes
Allergy InformationTree nuts (hazelnuts)
Yield4 servings

entry.title: Shizuoka Wasabi and Sansho Ice Cream with Toasted Nori Soil
entry.content:
Introduction

Welcome. In the quiet of the morning, I find that even the coldest elements can carry a hidden fire. Today, we explore the concept of piquant cooling. This ice cream is not a confection of sugar, but a meditation on the sharp, clean heat of Shizuoka wasabi and the electric tingle of sansho pepper, balanced by the gentle creaminess of my morning silken tofu. It is a dish that honors the transition of seasons—where the lingering chill of winter meets the spicy awakening of spring growth.

Ingredients

  • 300g fresh silken tofu, pressed lightly to remove excess water
  • 200ml organic soy cream or full-fat coconut milk
  • 100ml amazake (sweet fermented rice liquid)
  • 40g organic cane sugar or light agave
  • 2 tbsp freshly grated Shizuoka wasabi (grated in circles on an oroshigane)
  • 1 tsp ground green sansho pepper
  • 1/4 tsp sea salt
  • 1 sheet toasted nori, crumbled into fine dust
  • Fresh kinome leaves or shiso flowers for garnish

Instructions

  • Begin by passing the silken tofu through a fine mesh sieve or tamago-koshiki to ensure a texture as smooth as silk.
  • In a chilled bowl, whisk the soy cream with the sugar and sea salt until the sugar has completely dissolved and the mixture is slightly aerated.
  • Fold the sieved tofu and the amazake into the cream mixture with a bamboo spatula, moving with intention and care.
  • Gently incorporate the freshly grated wasabi and the sansho pepper. The fragrance should be sharp and citrusy.
  • Pour the mixture into an ice cream maker and churn until it reaches the consistency of soft-peak snow.
  • While the ice cream sets in the freezer for one hour, toast the nori sheet over a low flame until crisp, then grind it into a fine soil using a suribachi (mortar).
  • To serve, place a single, modest scoop into an asymmetrical stoneware bowl. Sprinkle the nori soil on one side and crown with a single kinome leaf.

As you finish, you will notice the heat does not burn; it glows. The umami of the nori and the sting of the wasabi fade into a clean, sweet memory. I hope this small bowl brings you a moment of stillness in your busy day.

Hiroshi

Additional Information
NutritionfactsCalories: 185kcal, Protein: 6g, Fat: 9g, Carbohydrates: 21g, Sodium: 150mg
Preparation Time20 minutes plus 4 hours freezing
Allergy InformationSoy
Yield4 small meditative servings

entry.title: Berbere-Spiced Cassava Gnocchi in Tangy Tamarind-Coconut Broth
entry.content:
Introduction

Hujambo! Today my kitchen breathes with the spirit of the Swahili coast and the spice-laden air of the highlands. I have gathered the earthiness of cassava and the fire of berbere to create a dish that is both piquant and deeply comforting. This gluten-free creation is an invitation to experience the Indian Ocean breeze in a single bowl, using traditional techniques to satisfy a modern palate.

Ingredients

  • 2 cups boiled cassava, mashed smooth with woody cores removed
  • 1/2 cup teff flour
  • 1 tablespoon berbere spice blend
  • 1 teaspoon sea salt
  • 2 cups fresh coconut milk, pressed this morning
  • 1/2 cup cooked pigeon peas (mbaazi)
  • 3 tablespoons tamarind paste diluted in 1/4 cup water
  • 2 minced pilipili chiles
  • 1 red onion, finely diced
  • 1 bunch sukuma wiki, thinly sliced
  • 1 tablespoon cold-pressed groundnut oil
  • Fresh lime wedges and kachumbari for finishing

Instructions

  • In a large mixing bowl, combine the warm mashed cassava, teff flour, berbere spice, and salt. Knead gently until a soft, pliable dough forms.
  • Pinch off small pieces of dough and roll them into bite-sized balls or traditional gnocchi shapes using your thumb.
  • Heat the groundnut oil in a heavy clay pot or jiko-safe pan. Sauté the onions and pilipili chiles until the onions are translucent and fragrant.
  • Pour in the coconut milk and the tamarind liquid, stirring gently to combine the creamy and tangy elements.
  • Bring the broth to a very gentle simmer. Carefully drop the cassava gnocchi into the liquid.
  • Cook for about 6 to 8 minutes; the gnocchi are ready when they float to the surface and have absorbed the flavors of the broth.
  • Fold in the pigeon peas and the sliced sukuma wiki, allowing the greens to wilt for just 2 minutes so they retain their vibrant color.
  • Ladle the dumplings and broth into bowls, top with a spoonful of fresh kachumbari, and add a final squeeze of lime before serving.

As the sun sets over the harbor, this bowl brings the warmth of the jiko right to your heart. It is a celebration of our heritage grains and the bold spices that have traveled our shores for centuries. I hope it brings a touch of Mombasa magic to your table today. Heri ya chakula!

Nia

Additional Information
NutritionfactsCalories: 385, Fat: 14g, Carbohydrates: 58g, Fiber: 9g, Protein: 7g
Preparation Time50 minutes
Allergy InformationContains coconut, groundnut oil (can substitute with coconut oil)

entry.title: Schiacciata di Ortone with Minted Cannellini Cream
entry.content:
Introduction

Benvenuti! Today the sun hangs low and golden over the hills, the perfect light for a mellow picnic under the shade of the ancient ilex trees. My garden has gifted me the first tender zucchine and their vibrant blossoms, so we shall make something that tastes of the Tuscan earth. This Schiacciata di Ortone is the heart of my picnic basket—a thin, crispy bread topped with the sweetness of the squash, paired with a velvety cannellini cream that we flavor with the wild mint growing by the stream. It is simple, it is honest, and it is meant to be shared with hands, not forks.

Ingredients

  • 500g Type 0 flour (or strong bread flour)
  • 350ml lukewarm spring water
  • 7g active dry yeast
  • 60ml premium extra virgin olive oil, plus extra for drizzling
  • 10g sea salt
  • 2 small young zucchine, sliced into paper-thin rounds
  • 6 fresh zucchini blossoms, stamens removed
  • 400g cooked cannellini beans (or one jar, rinsed)
  • 1 organic lemon, juiced and zested
  • 1 small clove of garlic, crushed
  • 1 large handful of fresh mint leaves
  • Flaky sea salt and cracked black pepper to taste

Instructions

  • In a large bowl, whisk the yeast into the lukewarm water and let it sit for 5 minutes until it begins to smile with tiny bubbles.
  • Add the flour and 20ml of olive oil. Mix by hand until a shaggy dough forms, then cover with a damp cloth and let rest for 30 minutes to autolyse.
  • Add the sea salt and knead the dough gently inside the bowl for a few minutes. It will be wet and sticky; this is correct for a light, airy crumb. Cover and let rise in a warm spot for 2 hours, or until doubled in size.
  • Preheat your oven to 220°C (430°F). If you have a baking stone or a heavy tray, let it get hot inside.
  • Generously oil a rectangular baking sheet. Gently stretch the dough onto the sheet using your fingertips to create small dimples.
  • Arrange the zucchini rounds and the blossoms across the top. Drizzle with more olive oil and a pinch of salt.
  • Bake for 20-25 minutes until the edges are deep gold and the zucchini is slightly charred.
  • While the bread bakes, prepare the cream. Place the cannellini beans, lemon juice, zest, garlic, mint, and the remaining olive oil into a mortar or blender. Process until silky smooth. Season with salt and pepper.
  • Allow the schiacciata to cool slightly, then slice into thick squares and serve with a generous dollop of the minted cream on the side or spread right on top.

Wrap this schiacciata in a clean linen towel while it is still warm to keep the edges soft. As you sit on your picnic blanket, let the smell of the rosemary and the cool mint cream take you to my hillside. This is the beauty of the cucina povera—taking the humblest beans and the morning's harvest to create a feast. Enjoy the stillness of the day. Buon appetito!

Isabella

Additional Information
NutritionfactsCalories: 340kcal | Carbohydrates: 52g | Protein: 11g | Fat: 10g | Fiber: 7g
Preparation Time2 hours 45 minutes
Allergy InformationContains Gluten. Contains Garlic.
Yield6 servings

entry.title: Binchotan-Grilled White Peach with White Miso and Amazake Cream
entry.content:
Introduction

The transition into the warmer months calls for a dessert that balances the heat of the fire with the cooling properties of silken tofu. Today, I offer a meditation on the white peach, or Momo. By lightly searing the fruit over binchotan charcoal, we awaken its natural sugars while adding a whisper of smoke. This is softened by a cream made from our morning tofu and the natural, non-alcoholic sweetness of fermented amazake. It is a dish of quiet contrasts.

Ingredients

  • 2 ripe seasonal white peaches
  • 150g fresh silken tofu, pressed for 30 minutes
  • 3 tablespoons house-made sweet amazake (rice ferment)
  • 1 tablespoon premium white shiro miso
  • 1/2 teaspoon sudachi juice or lime juice
  • 1 tablespoon toasted buckwheat groats (soba-cha)
  • 4 small purple shiso micro-leaves
  • A tiny pinch of flakey sea salt

Instructions

  • Prepare a small binchotan charcoal grill until the coals are glowing white and steady.
  • Slice the peaches in half and remove the pits with a precise cut, keeping the skin intact to hold the juices.
  • In a small stone mortar, blend the pressed silken tofu, amazake, and white miso. Work the mixture until it reaches a cloud-like consistency, then stir in the sudachi juice.
  • Place the peach halves cut-side down on the grill. Sear for 2 to 3 minutes until distinct grill marks appear and the fruit begins to soften slightly.
  • Transfer the warm peaches to an asymmetrical ceramic plate, resting them on their skins.
  • Spoon a generous dollop of the miso-amazake cream into the hollow where the pit once rested.
  • Sprinkle with toasted buckwheat for texture and a single flake of sea salt to elevate the umami.
  • Garnish with a single shiso leaf to provide a sharp, herbal finish.

As you take the last bite, notice how the saltiness of the miso lingers just long enough to invite another breath. This dish is not meant to overwhelm, but to refine your palate for the season ahead. May it bring you a moment of stillness.

Hiroshi

Additional Information

Preparation Time45 minutes

entry.title: Kaze no Kaori Shredded Root and Yuba Stew
entry.content:
Introduction

In the quiet of the morning, I look to the earth for grounding. Today, we embrace the concept of 'shredded' not as a lack of form, but as an unlocking of surface area for umami to cling to. This stew is a dialogue between the fibrous strength of the burdock root and the ethereal silkiness of fresh yuba. We use the sasagaki knife technique to shave the roots thin, allowing them to soften into a rich, kombu-fortified broth that warms the soul as the seasons shift.

Ingredients

  • 1 piece aged kombu (about 10cm)
  • 4 cups filtered water
  • 1 large burdock root (gobo), scrubbed and shredded sasagaki style
  • 2 large king oyster mushrooms, hand-shredded into long fibers
  • 100g fresh yuba (tofu skin), cut into thin ribbons
  • 1 medium carrot, prepared with katsuramuki then julienned
  • 2 tablespoons house-made dark hatcho miso
  • 1 tablespoon aged tamari
  • 1 teaspoon toasted sesame oil
  • A pinch of mountain pepper (sansho)
  • Fresh shiso leaves for garnish

Instructions

  • Steep the aged kombu in filtered water for at least 4 hours, then bring to a near-simmer over low heat and remove the kelp just before boiling.
  • Prepare the burdock root using the sasagaki method, shaving it into thin curls directly into cold water to prevent oxidation.
  • In a heavy-bottomed pot, lightly toast the shredded king oyster mushrooms with a drop of sesame oil until they release their moisture and begin to brown slightly.
  • Add the julienned carrots and the drained burdock root to the pot, stirring gently for two minutes to coat them in the mushroom essence.
  • Pour the prepared kombu dashi over the vegetables and simmer at a very low temperature for 15 minutes, ensuring the broth never reaches a rolling boil.
  • Gently fold in the yuba ribbons and the aged tamari, letting them warm through for 3 minutes.
  • Take a small ladle of the hot broth and whisk it into the hatcho miso until smooth, then stir the paste back into the stew.
  • Turn off the heat immediately to preserve the live enzymes and aroma of the miso.
  • Ladle into asymmetrical ceramic bowls and finish with a dusting of sansho and a single torn shiso leaf.

As you finish this bowl, notice the lingering hum of the hatcho miso and the earthiness of the gobo. It is a simple reminder that even the most humble roots, when treated with patience and precise knife work, can provide a feast as grand as any. May this bowl bring you a moment of zen in your busy day.

Hiroshi

Additional Information
NutritionfactsCalories: 185, Protein: 12g, Carbohydrates: 22g, Fiber: 8g, Fat: 6g
Preparation Time50 minutes
Allergy InformationSoy, Sesame
Yield2 servings

entry.title: Swahili Citrus Holiday Tagine with Saffron Pigeon Peas
entry.content:
Introduction

Karibu! Today, I am bringing the warmth of my Mombasa kitchen to your holiday table with a dish that captures the golden glow of the sun over the Indian Ocean. We are taking the humble pigeon pea and the sturdy cassava, then lifting them with the bright, zesty energy of seasonal citrus and the fiery depth of our coastal spices. It is a celebration of the trade winds and the red soil of the highlands, crafted to make your festive gathering feel both grounded and extraordinary.

Ingredients

  • 2 cups dried pigeon peas (mbazi), soaked overnight and boiled until tender
  • 1 large cassava root, peeled and cut into bite-sized cubes
  • 400ml fresh thick coconut milk (pressed from a mature coconut)
  • 2 tablespoons cold-pressed coconut oil
  • 1 large red onion, finely minced
  • 3 cloves garlic, crushed
  • 1 tablespoon fresh ginger, grated
  • 1 tablespoon berbere spice blend
  • 1 teaspoon ground cardamom
  • 1/2 teaspoon ground turmeric
  • Zest and juice of 2 Meyer lemons
  • Zest and juice of 1 blood orange
  • 1 fresh pilipili chile, slit lengthwise
  • 1/2 cup fresh pomegranate seeds
  • A handful of fresh coriander and mint, chopped
  • Sea salt to taste

Instructions

  • Heat the coconut oil in a heavy clay pot or deep pan over medium heat.
  • Sauté the red onion until it becomes translucent and soft, then add the garlic, ginger, and the whole pilipili chile.
  • Stir in the berbere, cardamom, and turmeric, allowing the spices to toast in the oil for about one minute until the aroma fills the air.
  • Add the cubed cassava to the pot along with a half cup of water; cover and steam for 12 minutes until the cassava starts to become tender.
  • Pour in the cooked pigeon peas and the thick coconut milk, stirring gently to combine.
  • Lower the heat and let the stew simmer for 15-20 minutes, allowing the sauce to thicken and the cassava to fully soften and absorb the spices.
  • Just before removing from the heat, stir in the Meyer lemon juice and the blood orange juice to brighten the flavors.
  • Prepare a quick citrus kachumbari by mixing the pomegranate seeds, fresh coriander, mint, and both citrus zests in a small bowl.
  • Serve the tagine hot, topped generously with the pomegranate-citrus kachumbari for a burst of holiday color and crunch.

As the charcoal in the jiko settles into glowing embers, I hope this dish fills your home with the scent of cardamom and citrus. Serve it with a smile and perhaps a warm chapati to scoop up every drop of that creamy coconut sauce. From my kitchen to yours, Heri ya Sikukuu—Happy Holidays!

Nia

Additional Information
NutritionfactsCalories: 410, Total Fat: 18g, Saturated Fat: 15g, Sodium: 120mg, Total Carbohydrates: 58g, Dietary Fiber: 12g, Protein: 11g
Preparation Time1 hour 10 minutes
Allergy InformationCoconut
Yield4 servings

entry.title: Mombasa Midnight Masala Sandwich
entry.content:
Introduction

Hujambo! Welcome to my coastal sanctuary. Today, I am bringing the warmth of the Mombasa sun and the depth of the Kenyan highlands to your plate. This isnt just a sandwich; it is a journey through the spice routes. We are taking the humble njahi—our nutrient-dense black bean—and elevating it with the fiery soul of berbere and the silky richness of coconut milk, all held together by a fermented teff-sourdough that whispers of our Ethiopian neighbors. It is crunchy, creamy, and carries the salt of the Indian Ocean breeze.

Ingredients

  • 2 thick slices of fermented teff-sourdough or artisanal sourdough bread
  • 1 cup njahi (black beans), soaked and boiled until tender
  • 1/2 cup fresh coconut milk, thick and creamy
  • 2 tablespoons roasted groundnuts, roughly crushed
  • 1 teaspoon berbere spice blend
  • 1/2 teaspoon cumin seeds
  • 1 cup sukuma wiki (collard greens), finely shredded
  • 1 small red onion, thinly sliced
  • 2 tablespoons tamarind paste diluted in water
  • 1 fresh pilipili chile, minced
  • A handful of fresh coriander leaves
  • 1 lime, halved
  • 1 tablespoon coconut oil
  • Sea salt to taste

Instructions

  • Heat coconut oil in a small clay pot or heavy pan and toast the cumin seeds until they fragrance the air.
  • Add the cooked njahi beans and berbere spice, stirring to coat every bean in the aromatic oil.
  • Pour in the coconut milk and simmer on low heat, mashing about a third of the beans to create a creamy, chunky texture. Season with salt and set aside.
  • In a small bowl, soak the red onion slices in the tamarind water with a pinch of salt and the minced pilipili to create a quick kachumbari-style pickle.
  • Flash-sauté the sukuma wiki in the same pan used for the beans just until they turn bright green and slightly tender but retain a snap.
  • Place your bread slices on a hot tava or cast-iron skillet until they are charred and golden on both sides.
  • Assemble the sandwich by spreading a generous layer of the coconut-njahi mash on one slice of bread.
  • Sprinkle the crushed groundnuts over the beans for a satisfying crunch.
  • Layer the sautéed sukuma wiki on top, followed by a heap of the tamarind-pickled onions and fresh coriander.
  • Squeeze fresh lime juice over the filling, top with the second slice of bread, and press down gently before slicing diagonally.

As you take that last bite, I hope you feel the red soil of the highlands and the rhythm of the Swahili coast. This sandwich is a bridge between tradition and the modern gourmet world. Serve it with a cold glass of tamarind juice and let the spices linger like a sunset over the water. Until we cook together again, heri ya kuonana!

Nia

Additional Information
NutritionfactsCalories: 480, Protein: 18g, Fiber: 14g, Fat: 22g (mostly medium-chain triglycerides from coconut), Carbohydrates: 56g
Preparation Time25 minutes
Allergy InformationGroundnuts (Peanuts), Gluten (if using blended sourdough bread)
Yield1 sandwich

entry.title: Shojin Umami-Katsu Breaded Salad
entry.content:
Introduction

In the quiet stillness of the morning, I pressed fresh silken tofu and harvested the last of the season's mizuna. Today's creation is a meditation on texture—a bridge between the crisp, golden crunch of panko and the fermented depth of our nukadoko. This breaded salad is not merely a meal; it is a celebration of the 'shun' or the fleeting peak of these ingredients. By lightly crumbing umami-rich shiitake and tofu in a katsu style, we create a warm contrast to the cool, crisp garden greens, all brought together by a gentle kombu dashi and miso emulsion.

Ingredients

  • 2 large thick-capped shiitake mushrooms, cleaned
  • 150g firm silken tofu, pressed and cut into batons
  • 1 cup fresh panko breadcrumbs, toasted until golden
  • 2 tablespoons rice flour
  • 3 tablespoons aquafaba (chickpea liquid) for dredging
  • 1 cup mizuna or wild arugula
  • 1 small daikon radish, sliced using katsuramuki technique into translucent ribbons
  • 2 pieces of nukazuke (rice-bran fermented) cucumber, thinly sliced
  • 1 tablespoon white miso
  • 1 tablespoon aged tamari
  • 1 teaspoon rice vinegar
  • 1/4 cup chilled kombu dashi
  • 1 teaspoon toasted sesame oil
  • A few pinches of black sesame seeds and fresh shiso leaves for garnish

Instructions

  1. Begin by preparing the dressing: Whisk together the white miso, aged tamari, rice vinegar, and chilled kombu dashi until smooth. Slowly drip in the toasted sesame oil while whisking to create a light emulsion. Set aside.
  2. Use a sharp knife to perform katsuramuki on the daikon, creating a long, paper-thin sheet, then slice into delicate ribbons. Place in ice water for 5 minutes to curl, then drain.
  3. Dredge the shiitake caps and tofu batons in rice flour, dip them into the aquafaba, and then coat thoroughly with the toasted panko breadcrumbs.
  4. Heat a small amount of neutral oil in a cast-iron pan or over binchotan charcoal. Gently sear the breaded shiitake and tofu until the crust is crisp and the interiors are warmed through. Slice the shiitake into thick strips.
  5. In a shallow, imperfect ceramic bowl, arrange a bed of fresh mizuna and the curled daikon ribbons asymmetrically.
  6. Nestled within the greens, place the warm breaded shiitake and tofu batons. Add the sliced nukazuke cucumber for a fermented acidic counterpoint.
  7. Drizzle the miso-dashi emulsion over the salad, ensuring the breaded elements retain some of their crunch.
  8. Finish with a scatter of black sesame seeds and hand-torn shiso leaves to add a bright, herbal aromatic.

As you finish this dish, notice how the lingering warmth of the binchotan-toasted crumbs softens into the brightness of the vinegar. It is my hope that this small bowl brings you a moment of zen in your busy day. May you carry the balance of these textures with you until the next season turns.

Hiroshi

Additional Information
NutritionfactsCalories: 285kcal, Protein: 12g, Carbohydrates: 34g, Fat: 11g, Fiber: 5g, Sodium: 620mg
Preparation Time45 minutes
Allergy InformationSoy, Gluten, Sesame
Yield1 serving

entry.title: Binchotan-Charred Daikon with Toasted Walnut Miso
entry.content:
Introduction

In the quiet dawn of the Kyoto hills, the daikon holds the last of winter's deep sweetness while reaching toward the first breath of spring. This dish, Furofuki Daikon, is a study in patience and the philosophy of shun. We simmer the radish until it becomes translucent and tender—a vessel for the deep umami of kombu—then crown it with a rich, hand-ground paste of toasted walnuts and my own aged red miso. It is a warm, grounding embrace that honors the transition of the seasons.

Ingredients

  • 1 large daikon radish (middle section preferred for sweetness)
  • 1 piece katsu-obushi-style kombu (approx. 6 inches)
  • 1 liter filtered spring water
  • 4 tablespoons aged red miso (hatcho miso)
  • 2 tablespoons mirin
  • 1 tablespoon coconut sugar or maple syrup
  • 1/2 cup toasted walnuts, finely crushed in a suribachi
  • 1 teaspoon fresh yuzu zest
  • 4 small sprigs of blanched nanohana (rape blossoms) or micro-greens
  • A pinch of sansho pepper

Instructions

  • Peel the daikon deeply to remove the fibrous outer skin, then cut into rounds approximately 2 inches thick.
  • Perform mentori by rounding off the sharp top and bottom edges of each disk with a knife to prevent them from breaking during simmering.
  • Place the daikon rounds in a heavy pot with the filtered water and kombu. Simmer over low heat for 45 to 50 minutes until a bamboo skewer glides through with zero resistance.
  • While the daikon simmers, prepare the walnut miso (kurumi-miso) by combining the red miso, mirin, and sweetener in a small pan over very low heat. Stir constantly until the mixture thickens and becomes glossy.
  • Fold the crushed walnuts into the miso paste and remove from heat.
  • Carefully remove the daikon from the dashi. For an optional touch of smoke, briefly sear one side of the daikon on a binchotan charcoal grill or under a broiler until lightly caramelized.
  • Place each daikon round in an imperfect ceramic bowl, add a small ladle of the warm kombu dashi, and spoon a generous dollop of the walnut miso on top.
  • Garnish with yuzu zest, a sprig of nanohana, and a dusting of sansho pepper.

As you lift your chopsticks, notice the steam rising—a fleeting moment of warmth in the cool spring air. This dish is simple, yet it contains the essence of the earth, the sea, and the passage of time. I hope this small meditation on the humble radish brings a sense of calm to your table today.

Hiroshi

Additional Information
NutritionfactsCalories: 195, Total Fat: 10g, Sodium: 640mg, Total Carbohydrates: 24g, Dietary Fiber: 5g, Protein: 7g
Preparation Time65 minutes
Allergy InformationSoy, Tree Nuts (Walnuts)
Yield4 servings

entry.title: Sun-Drenched Cauliflower and Farro Cacciatore
entry.content:
Introduction

Benvenuti! Today, my garden offers the last of the sun-drenched San Marzano tomatoes and the first sturdy heads of cauliflower. In the spirit of cucina povera, I have gathered these with farro—the ancient grain of my ancestors—to create a dish that is both humble and regal. This is a chunky, textured celebration of the harvest, where the bite of the cauliflower meets the chew of the grain, all bathed in a sauce that has simmered until it whispers of the wood-fire. It is simple, soul-warming, and finished with a pour of my neighbor's liquid gold olive oil.

Ingredients

  • 1 large head of cauliflower, cut into bite-sized florets
  • 1.5 cups pearled farro, rinsed
  • 3 tablespoons extra virgin olive oil, plus more for drizzling
  • 1 red onion, chopped into thick wedges
  • 3 cloves of garlic, smashed
  • 1 jar (28 oz) whole peeled San Marzano tomatoes, crushed by hand
  • 1/2 cup Taggiasca or Kalamata olives, pitted
  • 2 tablespoons salt-packed capers, rinsed
  • 1 teaspoon dried oregano
  • 1/2 cup toasted walnuts, roughly chopped
  • A handful of fresh flat-leaf parsley, torn
  • Sea salt and cracked black pepper to taste

Instructions

  • Preheat your oven to 200°C (400°F). Toss the cauliflower florets with two tablespoons of olive oil and a pinch of salt on a large baking sheet. Roast for 20-25 minutes until the edges are charred and caramelized.
  • While the cauliflower roasts, bring a large pot of salted water to a boil. Add the farro and cook until al dente, about 15-20 minutes. Drain and set aside.
  • In a heavy-bottomed pan or Dutch oven, heat the remaining tablespoon of olive oil over medium heat. Add the onion wedges and garlic, sautéing until they are soft and fragrant but not browned.
  • Stir in the hand-crushed tomatoes, olives, capers, and oregano. Let the sauce simmer gently for 15 minutes to allow the flavors to marry and thicken slightly.
  • Fold the roasted cauliflower and the cooked farro into the tomato sauce. Let it cook together for another 5 minutes, adding a splash of water if it becomes too thick.
  • Taste and adjust the seasoning with salt and plenty of black pepper. Remember, the capers and olives provide a natural saltiness.
  • Divide into bowls and top generously with the chopped toasted walnuts and fresh parsley. Finish with a final, generous drizzle of your best extra virgin olive oil.

Serve this in wide, shallow bowls and do not be shy with the black pepper. It is a dish that invites you to slow down and savor the changing seasons. Until the next harvest, buon appetito!

Isabella

Additional Information
NutritionfactsCalories: 425kcal, Protein: 14g, Fat: 19g, Carbohydrates: 58g, Fiber: 11g
Preparation Time45 minutes
Allergy InformationGluten (Farro), Tree Nuts (Walnuts)
Yield4 servings

entry.title: Smoked Masa Grits with Whipped Avocado and Charred Nectarines
entry.content:
Introduction

Morning, friends! Today we are bringing that golden coastal light right to your table. I am taking the soul of a Central Valley harvest and turning it into a creamy, dreamy brunch bowl that feels like a warm hug from the Pacific breeze. We are talking about smoky, stone-ground masa slow-cooked until it is velvet, topped with a whipped avocado silk and those gorgeous, end-of-season nectarines that are just begging for a little char. It is unfussy, vibrant, and exactly what your weekend needs.

Ingredients

  • 1 cup organic stone-ground masa harina
  • 3 cups filtered water or light vegetable stock
  • 2 tablespoons Sonoma extra virgin olive oil
  • 1 teaspoon smoked sea salt
  • 1/2 cup cashew cream (soaked cashews blended with water)
  • 2 ripe Ojai avocados
  • Juice of 1 lime
  • 1 tablespoon nutritional yeast
  • 2 firm-ripe nectarines, sliced into wedges
  • 1 Fresno chile, thinly sliced
  • A handful of fresh cilantro and mint leaves
  • 1 teaspoon agave nectar
  • 2 tablespoons toasted pepitas

Instructions

  • In a heavy-bottomed pot, whisk the masa harina into the water or stock. Bring to a low simmer over medium heat, stirring constantly to keep it smooth.
  • Reduce the heat to low, cover, and cook for about 20 minutes, whisking every few minutes until the mixture is thick and creamy. Fold in the olive oil, smoked salt, and cashew cream. Keep warm.
  • While the masa cooks, place the avocado flesh, lime juice, and nutritional yeast in a blender. Process until completely smooth and airy. Set aside.
  • Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat. Lightly brush the nectarine wedges with a tiny bit of oil and sear for 1-2 minutes per side until they have deep char marks and have softened slightly.
  • In a small bowl, toss the Fresno chiles with the agave nectar and a pinch of salt.
  • To serve, spoon the warm masa grits into shallow bowls. Add a generous swirl of the whipped avocado cream on top.
  • Arrange the charred nectarines and agave-soaked chiles over the cream. Garnish with fresh cilantro, mint, and toasted pepitas for a bit of crunch.

This is the kind of meal that makes you want to linger over a second cup of coffee while the sun hits the kitchen floor. It is grounded, bright, and pure California sunshine on a plate. I cannot wait to hear how it turns out in your kitchen. Enjoy every bite!

Emily

Additional Information

Preparation Time35 minutes
